extracted.intended_audience: litigators and attorneys handling expert witness admissibility in U.S. federal (and state) courts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating, challenging, and defending the admissibility of expert witness testimony under the Daubert trilogy and Federal Rule of Evidence 702, including factors, case law (Daubert, Joiner, Kumho), procedural mechanisms, and best practices for preparing experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the technique or theory can be tested and assessed for reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the expert’s technique or theory can be tested and assessed for reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus is on methodology rather than solely conclusions — whether the expert based its conclusion on sufficient facts or data and whether the conclusion is the product of reliable principles and methods reliably applied to the facts of the case. The Daubert 'litmus test' emphasizes testability and falsifiability (generating hypotheses and testing them).

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review and publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technique or theory has been subject to peer review and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review evaluates a scientific work by others in the field to ensure valid, reliable research is published; presence of peer-reviewed work supporting the methodology can help establish reliability. Lack of peer review can be a target for challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known or potential rate of error
rubrics_metrics.description: The known or potential rate of error of the technique or theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine the methodology for flaws that may produce errors. If an expert cannot provide a numerical error rate (or meaningful discussion of error), the court cannot analyze likelihood of error, which may render the evidence inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and maintenance of standards and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence and maintenance of standards and controls governing the technique or testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that there are standards and controls for the testing or technique, and that they were followed/maintained, supports reliability. Conversely, absence of standards or failures to adhere to them is a ground for exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: General acceptance in the scientific community
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the technique or theory has been generally accepted in the scientific community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While Daubert moved away from Frye's strict 'general acceptance' requirement, general acceptance remains one non-exhaustive factor and can raise concerns if absent — especially for well-established techniques (but it is not dispositive, particularly for novel methodologies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualification of the witness under Rule 702
rubrics_metrics.description: A witness must be 'qualified as an expert by knowledge, skill, experience, training or education.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualification is a threshold inquiry: the proponent must show the witness possesses sufficient credentials in the relevant area. Challenges may target lack of requisite knowledge, training, or relevant experience for the opinions offered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the expert's knowledge will help the trier of fact
rubrics_metrics.description: The expert’s knowledge must help the trier of fact to understand the evidence or to determine a fact in issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a relevance/helpfulness requirement under Rule 702; testimony that does not assist the jury or is not tied to a fact in issue can be excluded as irrelevant under Rule 702.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony based on sufficient facts or data
rubrics_metrics.description: The testimony must be based on sufficient facts or data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess whether the factual foundation for the opinion is adequate. Insufficient underlying facts/data in the report or testimony are a ground for exclusion or limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testimony is the product of reliable principles and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: The testimony must be the product of reliable principles and methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the principles/methods underlying the opinion are generally reliable for the task at hand. Reliability looks at soundness of the techniques, not simply the expert’s credentials or the conclusion reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliable application of principles and methods to the facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The expert's opinion must reflect a reliable application of the principles and methods to the facts of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if methods are generally reliable, the expert must apply them appropriately to the specific facts — courts will scrutinize the fit between method and case facts (see Joiner on analytical gaps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytical gap between data and opinion (Joiner/IPSE DIXIT rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may exclude an opinion if there is 'too great an analytical gap' between the data and the opinion; conclusions and methodology are not entirely distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joiner emphasizes that an expert cannot simply extrapolate from data by ipse dixit; there must be a demonstrable link between existing data and the expert's conclusions. Challenge the inferential steps and any unsupported extrapolations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of Daubert factors to non-scientific testimony (Kumho)
rubrics_metrics.description: Daubert factors for relevance and reliability may be applied to all expert testimony, including technical, or other specialized knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kumho extends the gatekeeper inquiry beyond 'scientific' testimony to experience- or skill-based opinions; courts may adapt the Daubert factors to the nature of the expertise (soft sciences, economics, industry practice, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for admissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The proponent of the expert testimony bears the burden to establish admissibility by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties offering expert evidence must demonstrate, by more likely than not, that the expert meets Rule 702 and Daubert criteria. This allocation affects strategy for preparing reports, declarations, and motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural forms/timing of a Daubert challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Daubert challenges can be made via a separate motion, as part of summary judgment, a motion in limine, an objection at the time the testimony is given, or in a post-trial motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the procedural vehicle that best fits the case timeline and evidentiary posture; many litigators prefer written pretrial motions (motion in limine or dedicated Daubert motion) to maximize research and evidentiary support. Challenges can also be preserved via contemporaneous objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological critique targets (how to attack methodology)
rubrics_metrics.description: When criticizing methodology, focus on: whether the type of testing conducted was done correctly; whether the potential rate of error is accurate; whether peer review/general acceptance supports the method; and whether inconsistent methodologies were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful Daubert motion targets specific methodological weaknesses and inconsistencies rather than blanket assertions. Identify the key assumptions, tests, and data that underlie the opinion and demonstrate flaws or unreliability with citations and expert rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert report disclosure requirement (Rule 26)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Rule 26, expert witnesses must disclose a report containing 'all opinions the witness will express and the basis and reasons for them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The expert report is the primary source opposing counsel will use in a Daubert challenge — ensure the report fully explains methods, data, literature relied upon, and the reasoning tying data to conclusions. Failure to disclose bases can be fatal or lead to exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and selection to minimize Daubert risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Select qualified experts with support in the relevant literature; ensure their opinions reflect the body of literature or identify why the literature does not apply; discuss case theme and strengths/weaknesses in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practices include vetting experts' credentials and litigation history, ensuring methodological transparency, anticipating weaknesses, preparing testimony to explain why methods are appropriate, and considering the judge’s history and preferences. Use vetting services and pre-retention analysis where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of appellate review — abuse of discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The appropriate standard of review for appellate courts reviewing district-court admissibility rulings is 'abuse of discretion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joiner clarifies appellate deference to district judges acting as gatekeepers; while appeals can contest exclusions, success requires showing the district court abused its discretion, which is a high threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective: exclude 'junk science' (scientific method and falsifiability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Daubert aims to prevent unreliable or 'junk science' from being heard as evidence; science here implies knowledge obtained through the scientific method (hypotheses generation and testing, falsifiability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for methodologies that produce testable, falsifiable results and that have undergone appropriate scientific rigor. Opinions characterized as theoretical, untested, or not grounded in recognized methodology are vulnerable to exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional variance in admissibility standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all jurisdictions apply Daubert uniformly — some states use Frye or modified approaches; a minority of states do not use Daubert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate local law: 5 states reportedly do not use Daubert and 16 use modified approaches. Tailor admissibility strategy to the applicable jurisdiction and any state-specific standards or precedents.
